P1_fx_receipts.question: Can resident individuals receive foreign currency for services or digital exports? Any conversion or repatriation rule?
P1_fx_receipts.answer: Yes. Under Banco de la República External Resolution 1 of 2018 (as compiled by DIAN), only the operations listed in art. 41 must be channelled through the FX market: goods imports and exports, external debt, foreign investment, Colombian investment abroad, financial investments abroad, guarantees and derivatives. Service exports are not on that list, so they are free-market operations. FX from them may be sold to other residents, used for permitted payments, kept abroad, or channelled voluntarily through the FX market (art. 82). Residents may freely hold bank accounts abroad (art. 81). Tax obligations still apply.

sources.title: Resolución Externa 1 de 2018, art. 41
sources.quote: ARTÍCULO 41. OPERACIONES. Las siguientes operaciones de cambio deberán canalizarse obligatoriamente a través del mercado cambiario: Concordancias 1. Importación y exportación de bienes.

sources.title: Resolución Externa 1 de 2018, art. 36
sources.quote: También formarán parte del mercado cambiario las divisas que, no obstante estar exentas de esa obligación, se canalicen voluntariamente a través del mismo.

P1_fx_receipts.notes: That service exports fall outside art. 41 is a reading of the closed list in art. 41 (the list names goods, not services). The search summary agreed; no BanRep FAQ stating it explicitly was captured.

P2_fcy_account.question: Can resident individuals hold a foreign-currency account locally?
P2_fcy_account.answer: Generally no, not in Colombia. Art. 83 of Resolution 1/2018 states that deposits or other financial operations in foreign currency in the country are not authorised, unless special rules provide otherwise (local FX deposits are reserved for listed cases, e.g. non-residents, travel and port businesses). Residents may instead freely hold FX accounts ABROAD (art. 81). If those accounts are used for operations that must be channelled, they must be registered with BanRep as 'cuentas de compensación' (art. 37).

L1_registration.question: Must an individual register a business to sell digital services/products? Simplest legal form?
L1_registration.answer: An individual (persona natural) can operate with a RUT (DIAN tax registration). Individuals with a Colombian cédula who do not carry on mercantile activities can register online, free, without a chamber-of-commerce process. Those doing mercantile activities register via the Chambers of Commerce or VUE. Gateways such as Wompi onboard 'Persona Natural' merchants on their RUT or cédula.

L2_tax_id.answer: The NIT (Número de Identificación Tributaria), obtained through RUT registration with DIAN. It identifies each registrant for tax, customs and exchange-control purposes. Individuals with a cédula can register online free of charge (identity is validated against the Registraduría).

L3_income_tax_foreign.question: Income tax on foreign-source income for residents; rates or special regimes
L3_income_tax_foreign.answer: Fiscal residents (183+ days in any 365-day period, or nationals meeting tests such as 50%+ of income from Colombia) are taxed on worldwide income. Progressive rates are 0% up to 1,090 UVT, then 19%, 28%, 33%, 35%, 37% and 39% (UVT = COP 52,347 for 2026). Alternative: the Régimen Simple de Tributación (RST) for individuals and companies with annual income up to 100,000 UVT. Its unified rate for professional, consulting and liberal-profession services is 5.9% (0–6,000 UVT), 7.3% (6,000–15,000), 12% (15,000–30,000) and 14.5% (30,000–100,000).

L4_vat_gst.question: VAT/GST: rate, registration threshold, treatment of exported digital services
L4_vat_gst.answer: The general IVA rate is 19%. Exported services are exempt with refund rights (ET art. 481(c)) when the service is provided in Colombia and used exclusively abroad by companies or persons with no business or activities in Colombia; formal requirements apply (Decree 1625/2016 rules). Individuals are 'not responsible' for IVA (no VAT obligations) if they meet all of: prior or current-year gross income from the activity below 3,500 UVT, no single taxed contract of 3,500 UVT or more, only one establishment, plus other conditions in ET art. 437 par. 3.

L5_data_protection.question: Data-protection law applicable to a small online business
L5_data_protection.answer: Ley 1581 de 2012 (general personal-data regime) applies to processing of personal data by natural or legal persons in Colombia, supervised by the SIC. Registration of databases in the National Register (RNBD) is required ONLY for companies and non-profits with total assets above 100,000 UVT and public entities (Decree 090/2018). Natural persons and micro and small companies are not required to register, though the substantive duties (authorisation, privacy policy, data-subject rights) still apply.

L6_consumer_ecommerce.question: Consumer-protection / e-commerce rules for online sales (refunds, disclosures)
L6_consumer_ecommerce.answer: Estatuto del Consumidor (Ley 1480 de 2011), art. 47: in distance or non-traditional sales a right of withdrawal (retracto) is implied. The consumer has 5 business days from delivery of goods, or from conclusion of a services contract. The provider refunds all sums without deductions; return costs are borne by the consumer. Exceptions include services already started with the consumer's agreement, personalised goods, goods that cannot be returned or perish, bets and lotteries, and goods for personal use. E-commerce sellers must disclose payment means, delivery times, and the retracto right and procedure.

W1_workarounds.question: Simple, legal routes around payment barriers for a beginner (no misrepresentation, nominees or sanctions evasion)
W1_workarounds.answer: Barriers: Stripe does not accept merchants here. Simple legal routes: (1) Sell digital products or software through a merchant of record: Paddle (software/SaaS only; each seller reviewed), Lemon Squeezy (bank payouts), Polar, Dodo Payments. The platform is the legal seller to your customers, handles card payments and consumer VAT/sales tax, and pays you out. You still declare the payouts as your income at home (see L3). (2) Sell services on Upwork, which is available here (not on its restricted list). Which withdrawal methods you get (bank, PayPal, Payoneer, etc.) depends on the country and shows in your account. (3) Creator income through the YouTube Partner Program (available here). (4) Paid apps and in-app sales through Google Play (merchant registration available here). (5) Client payments by PayPal (on PayPal's Payouts list as 'Send, receive, and withdraw'). (6) For direct clients, a bank transfer (SWIFT) into your own local account always works. Follow the local foreign-exchange rules (see P1) and keep invoices. Avoid: opening accounts with a foreign address, a relative's or friend's identity, or a VPN to look like you are elsewhere. It breaches platform terms (accounts and funds get frozen) and can break anti-money-laundering or sanctions law.
